paper_title: Breaking Diffusion: Parallel Reasoning with Draft Refinement

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Drafting an answer allows a reasoning model to reconsider each decision in the context of the others. Yet repeated diffusion denoising does not ensure that individually plausible token updates form a better answer together. We introduce Draft Refinement Language Models (DRLMs), which use a single denoiser to propose parallel revisions and evaluate a candidate draft. We train the denoiser to reconstruct every token from uniformly corrupted drafts, teaching both preservation and repair. Its predictions specify revisions directly, without a diffusion reverse transition. Evaluation requires a different use of these predictions: confidence in an existing token reflects both contextual support and evidence from observing the token itself. Using the known corruption process, we correct for this self-token evidence to estimate how well each token is supported by the prompt and the remaining draft. Aggregating these estimates yields a cavity energy computed in one forward pass, without an additional scoring model. Each round proposes a revision, reads the completed candidate in its revised context, and retains it only if its energy is lower. Across Countdown, Sudoku-Extreme, and Maze-Hard, our method outperforms autoregressive and discrete diffusion baselines. With 6M parameters, DRLM reaches 44.4% on Countdown-5 and 93.9% on Sudoku-Extreme. The results establish complete-draft parallel refinement as an effective alternative to reverse diffusion for complex reasoning.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: A draft can make its own mistakes visible. Consider rereading draft argument: its conclusion may conflict with an earlier claim, prompting us to reconsider step that seemed plausible on its own. The draft is not merely record of thought, but something to reason withits parts can be inspected, compared, and revised (Flower & Hayes, 1981; Kirsh, 2010). This suggests strategy for machine reasoning: construct complete but provisional answer early, then use the draft itself as context for refinement. complete draft makes the whole answer available as context, allowing earlier decisions to be reconsidered in light of later ones. Standard autoregressive models (Radford et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2020; Achiam et al., 2023; Touvron et al., 2023) commits earlier tokens before complete answer is available (Yao et al., 2023; Dziri et al., 2023). Discrete diffusion supports parallel prediction, but standard ancestral sampling constrains token updates through schedule-dependent reverse transitions (Austin et al., 2021; Lou et al., 2024; Sahoo et al., 2024; Nie et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025). Non-autoregressive refinement allows complete drafts to be revised directly (Lee et al., 2018; Savinov et al., 2021), yet individually plausible token updates do not necessarily produce more coherent answer. The challenge is not merely to revise, but to assess its revisions. Can the same model that proposes parallel revisions also estimate the resulting drafts contextual support in single forward pass? We introduce Draft Refinement Language Models (DRLMs), which use single denoiser to propose and evaluate revisions of complete answers. We train the model to reconstruct clean sequences from drafts corrupted by uniform token replacement, supervising every position. Because incorrect tokens are unmarked, the model must learn both what to preserve and what to repair. At inference, initialized from random tokens, its clean-token predictions directly generate revised draft: all positions are reconsidered in parallel using the same input context, without diffusion reverse transition. Correspondence to jaesangyu@kaist.ac.kr. Work done during an internship at Microsoft Research Asia. 1 Preprint. Under review. Using the same denoiser for evaluation requires separating contextual support from evidence supplied by the observed token itself. For example, in draft such as 2 + 3 = 6, the denoiser may favor the observed 6 because, under the corruption channel, observing token is far more likely when it is correct than when it is any particular alternativeeven when its prediction from the remaining context, 2 + 3 = , favors 5. Our correction removes this self-token advantage, estimating how well the context supports the drafts token rather than rewarding its mere presence. For Bayes-optimal denoiser, we show that dividing out the known self-token likelihood and renormalizing recovers the tokens cavity conditional (Mezard et al., 1987): its distribution given the prompt and all other noisy draft tokens. Applying this correction to the trained model yields estimates for every position from single full-draft read. Summing the negative log-probabilities assigned to the drafts tokens defines its cavity energy, learned, noise-smoothed pseudo-likelihood score (Besag, 1975). DRLM uses this score in proposereadretain generative loop. Each round partially re-noises copy of the retained draft to prevent draft converging to local optimum while preserving some of its context, then constructs candidate through direct parallel token predictions. fresh forward pass through the same model then scores the candidate at fixed read level, evaluating it in its revised context rather than reusing the predictions that produced it. The candidate replaces the retained draft only if its cavity energy is lower. All proposal and scoring passes count toward fixed inference budget, after which the decoder returns the lowest-energy draft. Our ablations show the benefits of retaining the best-scoring draft, refining it rather than restarting independently, and correcting the evaluation score for self-token evidence. Our contributions are as follows: One-pass contextual draft evaluation. We derive cavity decomposition of the full cleantoken posterior and use it to construct contextual draft score from one denoiser evaluation. The construction requires neither an architectural change nor separate evaluations with individual positions removed. Energy-controlled parallel refinement. We introduce proposereadretain generative loop in which single denoiser refines complete draft. Starting from randomly initialized tokens, each round proposes candidate via parallel token updates to partially re-noised retained draft and accepts the candidate only if the denoiser assigns it lower cavity energy. Improved reasoning performance. With 6M parameters, DRLM outperforms the evaluated autoregressive and discrete diffusion baselines on Countdown, Sudoku-Extreme, and Maze-Hard. It reaches 87.6% on Countdown-4, 44.4% on Countdown-5, 93.9% on Sudoku-Extreme, and 73.0% on Maze-Hard, exceeding the strongest diffusion baseline on each task by +14.3, +34.1, +28.4, and +33.7 percentage points.

Given schedule 1 = tT > > t0 = 0, standard ancestral decoding initializes each position independently from π and samples successive states from the learned reverse transitions. In standard masked diffusion, the schedule determines the probability of revealing masked position, while the model determines its revealed value. Once revealed, token is copied unchanged by subsequent reverse steps, even as its surrounding context changes (Sahoo et al., 2024). Remasking samplers relax this restriction by allowing visible tokens to return to the mask state (Wang et al., 2025b; Zheng et al., 2023; Ye et al., 2024). Uniform-noise diffusion permits repeated token revisions (Schiff et al., 2024), but the reverse kernel still constrains how predictions translate into changes. Under its plug-in parameterization, the probability of changing position is bounded by schedule-dependent ceiling, strictly below one for interior steps. Thus, in both standard ancestral decoders, clean-token predictions are mediated by diffusion transition rather than specifying the next sequence directly. Appendix gives the precise parameterizations and derives the masked revelation probability and uniform revision bound. From Draft Revision to Draft Evaluation. These constraints motivate refining complete drafts directly, letting clean-token predictions determine the next draft without reverse diffusion transition. Direct revision, however, does not decide whether revision should be kept: proposing candidate and evaluating it are separate decisions. Evaluation needs care, because full-posterior prediction treats each positions own token as evidence alongside the condition and the rest of the draft, so agreement with the current token does not by itself show contextual support.

Because single wrong position invalidates the entire solution, they test global planning rather than local pattern completion. See Appendix for experimental details. 4.1 COUNTDOWN Countdown is mathematical reasoning task that generalizes the classic 24 Game to arbitrary targets. Given set of input numbers, the goal is to construct an expression that evaluates to specified target using the operations {+, , , }. The task tests both arithmetic accuracy and planning: solver must identify useful intermediate quantities and combine them into valid solution. For example, given the numbers {97, 38, 3, 17} and target 14, one valid solution is 97 38 = 59, 59 17 = 42, 42 3 = 14. Setup. We use the Countdown splits released by Ye et al. sections.content: Model-bounded versus schedule-bounded generation. Figure 3(a) compares decoding trajectories on held-out Countdown-4 problems using identical backbone trained on the same data. At each step, we measure the fraction of positions agreeing with the decoders own final output. MGDM and UDLM closely track the schedule-dependent profiles αs and αs + (1 αs)/N , respectively: agreement increases with the prescribed keep probability rather than saturating early. In contrast, DRLM already agrees with its final output at 98.4% of positions after the first round, while every position remains eligible for revision. This shows that trust schedule conditions predictions rather than imposing reverse transition: the model directly determines which tokens to retain or replace. AccuracyCompute curve. Figure 3(b) tracks the Pass@1 of each decoders current output after every model call on Countdown-4 and Countdown-5, up to each methods default budget. On CD4, DRLM reaches 69.8% after one call and 81.1% after two, already above the final accuracy of UDLM (73.3%) and MGDM (43.7%), and later rounds raise it to 87.6%. UDLM instead stays near 50% for its first 16 steps and reaches its final accuracy only at the end of its schedule. On CD-5 the gap widens: DRLMs first call (14.0%) already exceeds the final accuracy of UDLM (6.7%) and MGDM (5.8%), and refinement keeps improving through all 32 rounds, to 44.4%. sections.title: 6 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Discrete Diffusion. Discrete diffusion learns reverse transitions for categorical corruption processes (Austin et al., 2021; Hoogeboom et al., 2021; Campbell et al., 2022; Lou et al., 2024), including masking (Sahoo et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024; Ou et al., 2025) and uniform replacement (Schiff et al., 2024; Sahoo et al., 2025), and has been scaled to billion-parameter language models (Nie et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025; 2026). MGDM adapts masked diffusion to parallel reasoning (Ye et al., 2024), adaptive unmasking orders improve masked diffusion on Sudoku (Kim et al., 2025b), and LDDM propagates continuous information alongside sampled tokens (Jo et al., 2026). Remasking and correction methods enable revision through remasking (Zheng et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025b), mixed maskuniform corruption (Von Rutte et al., 2025), explicit training on incorrect visible tokens (Zhang et al., 2025; Schiff et al., 2026), learned per-token quality scores that select tokens to remask (Kim et al., 2025a), or corrector steps that resample tokens from leave-one-out conditionals (Zhao et al., 2026). These methods retain generation based on diffusion transitions, remasking, or interleaved correction steps. Our method instead uses uniform corruption only to construct training drafts without sampling diffusion reverse transition, and it uses the channel likelihood to score complete candidates rather than to resample individual tokens. Non-Autoregressive Iterative Refinement. Complete-sequence refinement predates discrete diffusion: deliberation networks polish first-pass draft (Xia et al., 2017), and non-autoregressive translation refines drafts by iterative denoising (Lee et al., 2018) or by insertion and deletion edits (Gu et al., 2019). Mask-Predict (Ghazvininejad et al., 2019) and DisCo (Kasai et al., 2020) develop confidenceand context-dependent parallel updates. SUNDAE (Savinov et al., 2021) learns cleansequence reconstruction from uniformly corrupted inputs with its self-generated trajectories, and alternating corruption and denoising also defines generative Markov chains (Bengio et al., 2013). it Unlike these methods, which keep every revision, DRLM treats each revision as proposal: keeps the revised draft only if the same model assigns it lower energy. Recent structured reasoners scale test-time computation through weight-tied recurrence: HRM uses hierarchical recurrent states (Wang et al., 2025a), while TRM (Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2025) and PTRM (Sghaier et al., 2026) update both answer and latent states. DRLM instead uses the complete discrete draft itself as the recurrent state, making each rounds candidate directly interpretable.

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced Draft Refinement Language Models (DRLMs), which use single denoiser to propose and evaluate parallel revisions of complete drafts. All-position cross-entropy training on uniformly corrupted sequences teaches preservation and repair, enabling direct updates without diffusion reverse transition. Correcting predictions for the known self-token likelihood yields cavity estimates for one-pass contextual evaluation, supporting proposereadretain generative loop that returns the lowest-energy evaluated draft within fixed budget. Across Countdown, Sudoku-Extreme, and Maze-Hard, our method outperforms the evaluated autoregressive and discrete diffusion baselines. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining parallel revision with whole-draft evaluation for complex parallel reasoning. 9 Preprint. Under review.
